lesson1.title: Long Walk
acsAlignment: PA.IV.A Normal Takeoff and Landing introduction
repWalkthroughFocus: Visual check: airplane looks ready to move
beforeYouFly: This is your first flight. Stay calm.
The airplane responds to your inputs. Small movements matter.
KHMP Runway 24 is your home base. You'll always come back here.
Pattern altitude is 1,882 feet MSL. Field elevation is 882 feet MSL.
You don't need to sound like a pilot yet. You need to feel the airplane first.
mission: Complete the REP walk-around and prepare the aircraft to fly.
Taxi to Runway 24.
Take off and climb.
Keep KHMP nearby while you fly a simple circuit.
Return and land on Runway 24.
whatMattersToday: Remove chocks, tiedowns, pitot cover, and towbar.
Taxi without hitting anything.
Rotate at 55 KIAS.
Climb at 74 KIAS.
Keep the airport in sight.
Approach near 65 KIAS.
Land on the runway, not beside it.

targetNumbers.downwindKias: Not yet — just keep it safe

simpleFlightFlow: Walk around the airplane. Remove chocks, tiedowns, pitot cover, towbar.
Start the engine. Check that gauges look normal.
Taxi to Runway 24. Use rudder pedals to steer. Brakes when needed.
Line up on Runway 24 (heading about 240 degrees).
Add full power. Keep it straight with rudder.
Rotate at 55 KIAS. Climb at 74 KIAS.
Turn left when safe. Keep KHMP nearby. Opposite heading is about 060 degrees.
When ready to return, turn back toward Runway 24.
Reduce power. Aim at the runway. Keep speed near 65 KIAS.
Look toward the far end of the runway as you get close.
Flare gently. Reduce power to idle. Keep it straight with rudder.
Let it land. Don't force it down.
commonMistakes: Skipping the walk-around because it feels slow. Don't. REP tracks this.
Pulling back too hard on rotation. Gentle pressure, not yanking.
Letting speed get too slow or too fast. Check the airspeed indicator often.
Aiming at the ground instead of the far end of the runway during landing.
Trying to force the airplane onto the runway. Let it settle.
Forgetting to use rudder to keep it straight. Feet matter as much as hands.
doNotWorryAboutYet: Radio calls or ATC communication
Perfect rectangular pattern shape
Formal callouts like 'downwind' or 'final'
Flap settings or trim adjustments
Wind correction or crosswind technique
Emergency procedures beyond basic awareness
debriefReveal: The airplane felt busy because pitch, power, speed, and altitude were all moving at once.
You were managing everything manually. That's why it was hard.
Lesson 2 will introduce flaps and trim to calm things down.
The controls do what you tell them, but they don't think for you.
Every input has a consequence. Small corrections beat big ones.
You just flew an airplane. That's not nothing.

quizSeeds.question: What is the rotation speed (Vr) for the C172 in S2S?
quizSeeds.explanation: In S2S, the C172 rotates at 55 KIAS. This is the speed at which you gently pull back to lift off.

quizSeeds.question: What is the best rate of climb speed (Vy) for the C172 in S2S?
quizSeeds.explanation: Vy is 74 KIAS. This speed gives you the best rate of climb after takeoff.

quizSeeds.question: What is the approximate heading for KHMP Runway 24?
quizSeeds.explanation: Runway 24 is aligned at approximately 240 degrees. The runway number (24) represents 240 degrees divided by 10.

quizSeeds.question: Which of the following is part of the REP walk-around in Lesson 1?
quizSeeds.explanation: Lesson 1 focuses on removing chocks, tiedowns, pitot cover, and towbar as part of the REP walk-around.

quizSeeds.question: What is the target approach speed for landing in Lesson 1?
quizSeeds.explanation: The approach speed target is 65 KIAS. This helps maintain control during the landing phase.

lesson2.title: Configurator
repWalkthroughFocus: Configuration awareness: flaps position before takeoff
beforeYouFly: Lesson 1 felt busy because you were fighting the airplane the whole time.
Lesson 2 teaches the most important skill: knowing when to NOT land.
The go-around is not a failure. It's a decision. Most landing accidents happen because pilots force bad approaches.
Today you'll practice the GLGL sequence: Go-Around, Land, Go-Around, Land.
You'll fly 2 complete go-arounds with climbs back to pattern altitude, then 2 stable landings.
The decision point is ~100 feet AGL on final: stable approach = land, unstable = go around.
mission: Complete preflight walk-around.
Fly 2 go-around cycles (GA1 + Land1, then GA2 + Land2) around KHMP Runway 24.
Demonstrate stable approaches before landing (65 KIAS ±5, centered, descending smoothly).
Execute go-arounds when approach is unstable: full power, pitch up, climb back to 1,882 MSL, rejoin downwind.
Land safely 2 times.
whatMattersToday: Downwind speed: 90 KIAS. Approach speed: 65 KIAS ±5.
Pattern altitude: 1,882 feet MSL.
Decision AGL on final: ~100 feet. Stable = land, unstable = go around.
Go-around triggers: airspeed not 65, drifting off center, unstable descent, or 'doesn't feel right.'
Go-around procedure: POWER (full throttle, carb heat off), PITCH (arrest descent), CLEAN (flaps 20°), CLIMB (Vy 74 KIAS), REJOIN (downwind).
Flare decision: landing light visible 500-1,000 feet down runway means approach is stable.

targetNumbers.flapSettings: Incremental: 10° abeam numbers, 20° on base, 30° on final (or as needed)

simpleFlightFlow: Complete walk-around. Start engine. Taxi to Runway 24.
Take off. Climb to pattern altitude (1,882 feet MSL).
CYCLE 1 (GO-AROUND): Turn downwind. Set power 90 KIAS. Abeam numbers: flaps 10°.
Turn base. Flaps 20°. Turn final. Flaps 30°. Aim for 65 KIAS.
At ~100 feet AGL on final: approach unstable? FULL POWER → PITCH UP → CARB HEAT OFF → FLAPS 20° → CLIMB AT 74 KIAS → REJOIN DOWNWIND.
Now back at downwind, repeat approach.
CYCLE 2 (LANDING): Downwind setup same. Final approach. At ~100 feet: approach STABLE? → Flare. Land.
After landing, add power for next takeoff.
CYCLE 3 (GO-AROUND): Depart again, repeat first go-around cycle.
CYCLE 4 (LANDING): Final approach. Stable? → Flare. Land. Done.
commonMistakes: Waiting too long to go around. If it doesn't feel right at 100 feet, don't wait until 50 feet. GO AROUND.
Not using full power on go-around. Half-power = sluggish climb = stall risk. Full throttle (2,500 RPM).
Forgetting carb heat on go-around. Push it in (cold air) so full power works efficiently.
Pulling nose up too hard on go-around. Gradual back pressure, not abrupt. Stall is worse than hard landing.
Retracting flaps too early. Wait for positive climb rate before moving flaps from 30° → 20°.
Not checking speed/altitude before landing. Unstable approach = go around. Stable = land.
Chasing airspeed with pitch. Power controls altitude, pitch controls speed in the pattern.
doNotWorryAboutYet: Perfect go-around procedures (e.g., gear/flap sequence for complex aircraft—C172 is simple).
Crosswind limits. L2 is calm conditions only.
Go-around on base leg or earlier phases. This lesson focuses on final approach decisions.
Missed approach procedures (instrument flying). S2S is VFR only.
Engine failure procedures. L3 covers stalls; L4 covers engine-out emergency landing.
debriefReveal: The go-around is the most important landing skill. You demonstrated two full go-around cycles today.
Going around is not a failure. It's a safety decision. You will never be criticized for a go-around.
The decision point is ~100 feet AGL on final. Stable approach = land. Unstable = go around immediately.
POWER, PITCH, CLEAN, CLIMB, REJOIN is the mental model for every go-around. Speed and precision matter less than decision-making.
Go-around triggers: airspeed not 65±5, drifting off center, unstable descent, late flare recognition, or 'doesn't feel right.'
You must demonstrate 2 successful go-arounds AND 2 stable landings before Arc 1 is complete.
L3 will teach slow flight and stalls so you understand why unstable approaches are dangerous at low altitude.

quizSeeds.question: At what altitude on final approach do you make the decision to land or go around?
quizSeeds.explanation: The decision point is ~100 feet AGL on final. At this altitude, you assess: stable = land, unstable = go around. Waiting until 50 feet gives you too little time to climb.

quizSeeds.question: What is the first action in a go-around?
quizSeeds.explanation: The first action is full throttle (2,500 RPM). This gives you the power needed to climb against the drag of extended flaps and slow airspeed.

quizSeeds.question: What does 'CLEAN' mean in the go-around sequence POWER, PITCH, CLEAN, CLIMB, REJOIN?
quizSeeds.explanation: CLEAN means retracting flaps gradually: start at 30°, move to 20°, then 10°, finally 0°. Don't dump all flaps at once—that causes a sudden sink.

quizSeeds.question: What is a sign that your approach is UNSTABLE and you should go around?
options: You are 500 feet above the runway
Your airspeed is 65 ±5 KIAS and you're centered
Your airspeed is not 65 KIAS or you're drifting off centerline
You can see the runway clearly
quizSeeds.explanation: Unstable signs: airspeed not 65 KIAS (too fast or too slow), drifting off centerline, altitude not descending smoothly, or anything that feels wrong. All of these trigger a go-around.

quizSeeds.question: What is the target climb speed during a go-around?
quizSeeds.explanation: During climb on go-around, target Vy (74 KIAS). This is the best rate of climb speed for the C172. It gets you back to pattern altitude fastest while maintaining safe margin from stall.

lesson3.title: Edge of the Envelope
repWalkthroughFocus: Aircraft state check before unusual attitudes
Systems awareness during high workload maneuvers
beforeYouFly: Lesson 2 revealed why configuration matters. Today you'll learn where the edges of safe flight are.
Slow flight means the controls feel mushy. The airplane still flies, but it's less responsive.
A stall doesn't mean the engine quits. It means the wing stops flying normally.
Recovery from a stall is simple: reduce angle of attack, add power, level wings, recover climb.
Steep turns need extra back pressure to maintain altitude. Don't pull harder when already slow.
Preflight and walk-around still matter, even before maneuver practice.
mission: Complete preflight walk-around.
Depart KHMP Runway 24 to the practice area.
Practice slow flight: maintain altitude and heading at minimum controllable airspeed.
Practice power-off stall recovery: recognize the stall, recover promptly.
Practice steep turns: 45° bank, maintain altitude.
Return to KHMP and land on Runway 24.
whatMattersToday: Slow flight: controls feel mushy, high angle of attack, maintain altitude.
Stall warning: buffet, nose-high attitude, loss of control effectiveness.
Stall recovery sequence: 1) reduce angle of attack (push forward), 2) add full power, 3) level wings, 4) recover to climb.
Steep turns: 45° bank requires back pressure to hold altitude. Don't stall it.
Altitude awareness during maneuvers.
Preflight discipline before every flight.

targetNumbers.practiceAltitudeMsl: 3,500 feet MSL or higher (at least 1,500 AGL)
targetNumbers.stallRecoveryPriority: 1) Reduce AOA, 2) Full power, 3) Level wings, 4) Climb

simpleFlightFlow: Complete walk-around. Start engine. Taxi to Runway 24.
Take off. Climb to practice altitude (3,500 feet MSL or as assigned).
Maneuver 1: Slow Flight. Reduce power, maintain altitude, slow to 50-55 KIAS. Feel mushy controls. Maintain heading and altitude. Recover: add power, lower nose, accelerate.

Maneuver 2: Power-Off Stall. Reduce power to idle. Raise nose to induce stall. Feel buffet. Recognize stall. Recover: 1) push forward (reduce AOA), 2) full power, 3) level wings with rudder/aileron, 4) establish climb.
Maneuver 3: Steep Turn. Establish 45° bank. Add back pressure to hold altitude. Complete 360° turn. Roll out on entry heading.
Return to KHMP. Enter pattern. Land on Runway 24.
commonMistakes: Confusing a stall with engine failure. The engine is fine. The wing stopped flying.
Pulling harder when already slow. This makes the stall worse.
Not reducing angle of attack first during stall recovery. Push forward before adding power.
Forgetting rudder coordination during stall recovery. Keep wings level with rudder.
Not using enough back pressure in steep turns. The airplane will descend if you don't pull.
Skipping preflight because 'it's just maneuvers.' Preflight always matters.
doNotWorryAboutYet: Perfect altitude control during slow flight (±100 feet is fine for now)
Perfect rollout heading on steep turns
Power-on stalls or accelerated stalls
Spin awareness or spin recovery (not part of Arc 1)
Complex aerodynamics theory. Just feel it and recover.
debriefReveal: Slow flight shows you where the airplane becomes less responsive. Stay aware of airspeed.
Stalls happen when the wing's angle of attack is too high. Reduce it by pushing forward.
The stall recovery is always the same: 1) reduce AOA, 2) power, 3) level wings, 4) climb.
Steep turns require back pressure because the vertical component of lift is reduced in a bank.
Pulling harder when slow makes things worse. Add power and reduce angle of attack first.
Lesson 4 is your Arc 1 Check Flight. You'll link everything you've learned under pressure.

quizSeeds.question: What does 'slow flight' mean?
options: Flying at minimum controllable airspeed where controls feel mushy
quizSeeds.explanation: Slow flight means flying at minimum controllable airspeed (50-55 KIAS for C172). Controls feel mushy but the airplane still flies.

quizSeeds.question: What is the first action in a stall recovery?
options: Reduce angle of attack by pushing forward
quizSeeds.explanation: First, reduce angle of attack by pushing the yoke forward. This unstalls the wing. Then add power, level wings, and climb.

quizSeeds.question: Does a stall mean the engine has failed?
options: No, stall means the wing has stopped flying normally due to high angle of attack
quizSeeds.explanation: A stall is an aerodynamic condition where the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack. The engine is still running.

quizSeeds.question: Why do steep turns require extra back pressure?
options: Because the vertical component of lift is reduced in a bank
quizSeeds.explanation: In a steep bank, lift is tilted. Less vertical lift is available to counteract weight, so you pull back to maintain altitude.

quizSeeds.question: What should you NOT do during a stall recovery?
quizSeeds.explanation: Pulling harder increases angle of attack and worsens the stall. Push forward first to reduce AOA and unstall the wing.

lesson4.title: Arc 1 Check Flight
lesson4.mode: Free Tower Mode with Check Flight Discipline
repWalkthroughFocus: Complete preflight as if it's a real checkride
beforeYouFly: This is your Arc 1 Check Flight. You've learned the pieces. Now link them together.
You'll fly 5 touch-and-goes on Runway 24. Repeatability matters more than one pretty landing.
After the 5th touch-and-go, you'll simulate an engine failure and land on Runway 06.
Runway 06 is the opposite direction (heading ~060°). It's emergency-only.
Best glide speed is 68 KIAS. Don't stretch the glide by pulling. You'll stall.
This lesson requires a passing quiz score, a flight score >= 3, and debrief review to unlock Arc 2.
Preflight walk-around is mandatory. Treat this like a real flight.
mission: Complete full preflight walk-around with REP discipline.
Taxi to Runway 24.
Perform 5 consecutive touch-and-goes on Runway 24.
On the 5th touch-and-go after liftoff, simulate engine failure.
Establish best glide (68 KIAS) and land on Runway 06.
Complete shutdown and debrief.
whatMattersToday: Preflight discipline: no shortcuts.
Pattern consistency: downwind 90 KIAS, approach 65 KIAS, pattern altitude 1,882 MSL.
Touch-and-go technique: land, add power smoothly, climb out.
Repeatability: 5 safe landings, not just 1 lucky one.
Emergency response: recognize failure, establish best glide (68 KIAS), pick Runway 06, fly it all the way.
Do not stretch the glide. Best glide speed or you stall.
Obstacle awareness near Runway 06: approximate elevation ~920 feet MSL (pending verification).

targetNumbers.runway: KHMP Rwy 24 for patterns, Rwy 06 for emergency landing

simpleFlightFlow: Complete full REP walk-around. Remove chocks, tiedowns, pitot cover, towbar.
Start engine. Check all indications normal.
Taxi to Runway 24.
Touch-and-Go 1: Takeoff, pattern, landing, add power, go.
Touch-and-Go 2: Repeat. Focus on consistency.
Touch-and-Go 3: Repeat. Stable approaches.
Touch-and-Go 4: Repeat. Nail the speeds.
Touch-and-Go 5: Takeoff normally. After liftoff (~400 AGL), engine failure simulation begins.
Emergency procedure: throttle idle (simulated failure). Establish best glide 68 KIAS immediately.
Turn toward Runway 06 (heading ~060°). You're already in the vicinity.
Fly best glide. Do not pull to stretch it. Clear obstacles (~920 MSL).
Land on Runway 06. Rollout. Clear runway. Shutdown.
Debrief: review what worked, what didn't.
commonMistakes: Rushing the preflight. Don't. This is a check flight.
Inconsistent pattern speeds. Lock in 90 KIAS downwind, 65 KIAS final.
Bad first landing and giving up. Each landing is separate. Nail the next one.
Panicking during the simulated engine failure. It's simulated. Fly the airplane.
Pulling to stretch the glide during emergency. You'll stall. Fly 68 KIAS.
Forgetting Runway 06 heading (~060°). Know where it is before the emergency.
Not clearing obstacles near Runway 06. Maintain best glide and clear terrain.
doNotWorryAboutYet: Perfect pattern rectangles. Consistency matters more than shape.
Radio communication. Still Free Tower Mode.
Short or soft field technique. Not tested in Arc 1 check.
Complex emergency checklists. Just fly best glide and land.
Checkride-level perfection. Arc 1 is crawl level. Arc 5 is checkride level.
debriefReveal: You just linked preflight, pattern work, and emergency response under pressure.
Repeatability is what makes a pilot safe, not one lucky landing.
The emergency wasn't about panic. It was about discipline: best glide, pick a spot, fly it.
Runway 06 is emergency-only, but now you know it's there.
Arc 1 is complete. You have mechanical intimacy with the C172.
Arc 2 begins pattern mastery: rectangular precision, callouts, and wind correction.
You're no longer a passenger. You're a student pilot.

quizSeeds.question: What is the best glide speed for the C172 in S2S?
quizSeeds.explanation: Best glide speed is 68 KIAS. This gives maximum glide distance in an engine-out scenario.

quizSeeds.question: What is the heading for KHMP Runway 06?
quizSeeds.explanation: Runway 06 is aligned at approximately 060 degrees. It's the opposite direction from Runway 24 (240°).

quizSeeds.question: How many touch-and-goes are required in Lesson 4 before the simulated engine failure?
quizSeeds.explanation: You perform 5 touch-and-goes on Runway 24. After the 5th takeoff, the engine failure simulation begins.

quizSeeds.question: What should you do if you try to stretch the glide by pulling back during an engine failure?
options: You'll risk a stall and lose altitude faster
quizSeeds.explanation: Pulling back to stretch the glide reduces airspeed below best glide, risking a stall. Maintain 68 KIAS for best performance.

quizSeeds.question: What does Lesson 4 require to unlock Arc 2?
options: Flight score >= 3, quiz pass, and debrief viewed
quizSeeds.explanation: Arc 1 gate requires: flight score >= 3, quiz passed, and debrief viewed. All three must be completed.
